newsitem.title: THAILAND: Ex-Khmer Rouge group sceptical over Pol Pot report.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Khmer Rouge group sceptical over Pol Pot report.

text.p: A group of former Khmer Rouge guerrillas who split with the movement last year said it was sceptical of reports that its infamous leader Pol Pot was on the run and had taken several of his comrades hostage.

In the first official comment from former members of the guerrilla organisation, a spokesman for the Democratic National United Movement headed by former Khmer Rouge foreign minister Ieng Sary also said it would not help the government resolve the situation.

"We are sceptical about the reports and have already told the Cambodian coalition government that we will not be getting involved even if the reports were true," DNUM spokesman Mitr Yaem told Reuters by telephone from Pailin, the former guerrilla headquarters in northwestern Cambodia.
"We told the government that we will not get involved with them (Khmer Rouge) anymore," he said.

Cambodia's first premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh and his senior military aide have said that Pol Pot, his health failing, killed his own defence minister Son Sen and his family and then fled his northern stronghold of Anlong Veng with up to 300 hardline followers.
They said Pol Pot had taken Khmer Rouge nominal leader and front man Khieu Samphan and two other senior officials hostage while on the run.

Pol Pot was now holed up in thick jungle near Anlong Veng, surrounded by about 1,000 of his former guerrillas who had now defected to the Cambodian government, military officials said on Saturday. No new information on the situation was available on Sunday.

The reports have been greeted with some scepticism, with many analysts wondering whether the episode may have been cooked up to differentiate the totally unpalatable Pol Pot from his marginally less despised comrades so that they can join the political mainstream.
More than one million people are estimated to have died through starvation, executions, hard labour and disease during the Khmer Rouge's disastrous experiment with total communism.
Ieng Sary's break with the Khmer Rouge last August was the catalyst for thousands of defections, and analysts now estimate only about 2,000 hard-line rebels remain.
While his troops have merged with the government, the DNUM has remained an independent political arm.
Under his peace agreement with the government, Ieng Sary's former commanders retain administrative control over their territory in Cambodia's northwest.
Ieng Sary, who is Pol Pot's brother-in-law, was not available for comment.
